source_text: Quod quoniam a nobis ea facultate, quam veritas suppeditavit, ostensum est, prudens lector super hoc ulterius dubitare non debet; ubicumque hoc in Traduciani scriptis occurrerit (sine quo tamen hiare non potest), nihil moveat audientes, sed in verecundiam protestetur auctoris; nos autem id deinceps, si res compulerit, necessaria brevitate tangemus. Arguit ergo quod dixi: Ista corporum commixtio, cum calore, cum voluptate, cum semine a Deo facta, et pro suo modo laudabilis approbatur [n14] . Sed praeteriit illud quod subdidi: De re autem, quae instituta naturaliter, fitaliquando etiam amplum munus piorum, diabolus sibi nec tua fronte audet aliquid vindicare.
pass_a_gloss: Which since it has been shown by us with that facility which the truth supplied, a prudent reader ought not to doubt further upon this; wherever this shall have occurred in the Traducian's writings (without which nevertheless he cannot gape), let it move the hearers nothing, but protest into the author's shame; but we thereafter, if the matter shall have compelled, will touch it with necessary brevity. He therefore accuses what I said: That mingling of bodies, with heat, with pleasure, with seed made by God, is approved also praiseworthy according to its measure. But he passed over that which I subjoined: But about a matter which, instituted naturally, is sometimes even an ample gift of the pious, the devil dares not even with your forehead claim anything for himself.

lemmas.lexica: Julian's polemic label for teachers of tradux peccati
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Since we have demonstrated this with the ability truth supplied, the discerning reader should have no further doubt about it. Wherever this appears in the writings of the advocate of inherited sin—who nevertheless cannot open his mouth without it—let it neither disturb listeners nor do anything except testify to its author’s shame. We will henceforth touch on it, if the matter compels us, with the brevity required. He attacks my statement: ‘This union of bodies, created by God with its heat, pleasure, and seed, is shown to be praiseworthy according to its own measure’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.25). But he passed over what I added: ‘Concerning something instituted by nature which sometimes also becomes a generous gift to the devout, even the devil does not dare to claim anything for himself with your effrontery.’

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
